finding.claim: POST /settings/email is decorated with login_optional instead of login_required, so unauthenticated requests reach the account-changing operation with g.uid = None. Other settings routes (e.g. /settings/password) use login_required, which shows the intent. Impact depends on how set_email handles a None uid: it may fail, or it may update an unintended or null-keyed record (e.g. WHERE id IS NULL or an anonymous record). The email-change endpoint is the usual first step in account takeover (via password reset). The code as written lacks a guard; the stub set_email is empty, so the impact is not fully demonstrable.
finding.source: Unauthenticated HTTP POST to /settings/email with no session cookie
finding.sink: set_email(g.uid, ...) at routes.py:37, a state-changing account operation

trace.note: login_optional sets g.uid = session.get('uid'), which is None when there is no session, and never aborts
change_email is wrapped with login_optional, not login_required
set_email is called with the possibly-None g.uid; there is no check that it is set

finding.guards_checked: login_required is not applied. login_optional does not enforce authentication. There is no inline check of g.uid in the handler. No CSRF protection is visible in the file. Flask has no global before_request guard in this file.

verdict.guard_found: none (login_optional at routes.py:19-25 only sets g.uid and never aborts; no inline g.uid check; no before_request hook)
verdict.reason: routes.py:35 applies login_optional (routes.py:22 sets g.uid=None without aborting) so an anonymous POST reaches set_email(g.uid, ...) at routes.py:37, unlike /settings/password at routes.py:42 which uses login_required (routes.py:11-12 aborts 401); the set_email stub at routes.py:48 is empty, so the impact is not demonstrable, but the missing auth guard is real.
